title: The Ascent and Fall of Nahusha
body:
The Ascent and Fall of Nahusha

The Throne of Heaven

King Nahusha, the son of Ayus, was initially celebrated throughout the three worlds as an exceptionally righteous, just, and powerful monarch. He ruled his earthly subjects with absolute fairness, performing countless sacrifices, venerating his ancestors, and strictly following the injunctions of the scriptures. Through these rigorous spiritual disciplines, he accumulated an immense, blazing store of spiritual merit (punya) that made his personal effulgence rival that of the gods.
During this period, Indra, the king of the gods, was forced to flee his heavenly capital and go into hiding. He had committed the sin of unrighteously slaying the demon Vritra through deceit, and to expiate this transgression, he reduced himself to the size of an atom, hiding inside a single fibre of a lotus stem in the remote Manasarovar lake. Finding heaven leaderless and vulnerable to the attacks of the Asuras, the gods and sages performed a great search for a mortal of sufficient spiritual merit to occupy the throne of heaven. Their eyes fell upon King Nahusha. With great ceremony, they invited him to ascend the celestial throne and rule the three regions as the temporary Indra.

The Corrosion of Pride

For a brief period, Nahusha ruled heaven with justice, supported by his accumulated merit. However, sudden, absolute prosperity is a dangerous spiritual test. Surrounded by the intoxicating, ethereal pleasures of heaven, Nahusha's mind began to decay. He lost his humility, forgot the sages' teachings, and became a victim of intense Ahankara—spiritual egoism. One afternoon, while strolling through the gardens of heaven, he saw Sachidevi, the chaste and beautiful wife of the fugitive Indra, and was instantly seized with lawless, lecherous desires. Armed with the power of his new office, he commanded the gods: 'Why has not Sachidevi come to my mansion? Am I not the king of heaven now? Send her to my quarters immediately.'
Sachidevi, terrified and indignant, sought refuge under the roof of the preceptor Brihaspati, who promised her absolute protection. When the gods and sages went to Nahusha, begging him to conquer his desires and respect the sacred laws of marriage, the infatuated king mocked them, pointing out that previous Indras had committed similar moral transgressions. Seeing his stubborn madness, Brihaspati advised Sachidevi to employ a clever stratagem. She went to Nahusha and said: 'Lord, I shall gladly accept you as my husband, but first, I have a deep desire. You must come to my mansion in a grander style than any deity before you. Let your palanquin be carried on the shoulders of the seven great Rishis (Saptarishis), who are the absolute masters of the Vedas.'
Blinded by lust and arrogance, Nahusha agreed, believing that his power was absolute. He summoned the Saptarishis, including the mighty Sage Agastya, and ordered them to carry his palanquin. At this terrible sacrilege, the three worlds stood aghast. As they proceeded, Nahusha, inflamed by thoughts of the beautiful Sachidevi waiting for him, became impatient with the slow pace of the sages. He began to goad them, and in a moment of supreme, mad wickedness, he kicked the head of Sage Agastya with his foot, shouting 'Sarpa! Sarpa!' (meaning 'move faster, move like a snake').
The wrath of a sage who has attained the absolute power of brahmacharya is more potent than any physical weapon. Agastya, looking upon the fallen king with blazing eyes, pronounced a terrifying curse: 'Meanest of the mean, because you have kicked a sage and desecrated the spiritual order, do thou fall instantly from heaven and become a python (sarpa) on earth!' Instantly, Nahusha's celestial form withered, his merit evaporated, and he fell headlong through the clouds to live as a python in the dust of the forest, condemned to wait thousands of years for Yudhishthira's wisdom to release him. This remains a devastating lesson: that no amount of intellectual learning or ritual merit can save a soul that has succumbed to the illusion of pride.
